segment:
Gerald’s companion came around the corner now, a young woman with her hair tied back; she was wearing an orange dress, carrying an empty wine glass.
“And this is Adrian,” Gerald finished, “and I don’t have to tell you who this is.”

The woman in orange smiled and came forward to shake hands. “Livia,” she said.

As Livia turned away and raised her hand in greeting toward Mara, the woman in brown—who was still nameless, still unknown—glanced briefly back over her shoulder with a slightly puzzled look, as though she’d only now registered how many people there were in here, all of them not her. And then she turned fully to face the gathering and moved closer to the low table at the end of the couch.

In the empty wine glass.
A drop of liquid.

An unnamed older catering worker—not Livia—retrieved the abandoned glass without acknowledgment while its owner's conversation continued. Through observable action, Mara noticed who assumed whose labor. End on that concrete recognition before anyone turned it into a lesson.
text:
When Mara walked into the common room at six fifteen, someone was already there. Someone younger, it seemed.
She couldn’t make out the face behind the blond hair. But the body was fine enough, leaning back on the couch with bare legs crossed and arms flung in opposite directions, one palm pressing the padded wall and the other wrist resting on the low table beside him.
She stood stock-still by the doorway for a moment, aware of her breath and of his awareness that she was here. He stirred and tilted his head; a face turned toward her, expressionless.

The two pairs of eyes held each other through an entire exhale.
And then the young man had pushed himself up on the armrests, stretched to his full height, and strolled over to shake her hand.
“Mara?”
He was closer than she would have guessed from where he’d been sitting, broad-shouldered and strong-chinned in a white T-shirt, grinning at her through dark-framed glasses as he reached out for the handshake. She took it.
“Jonah,” he said.
“Hello,” she replied, and then they stood there, still shaking hands, not knowing what to do next.

And that was when a door opened down the hallway behind her, releasing two voices into the room. One female, one male; one asking a question, the other replying; neither loud nor excited, just casual conversation. Jonah released her hand and turned away to look down the hall at them.
When Mara heard the voices and followed his gaze, she saw one young man who wasn’t Jonah, but close in size and shape; he had brown hair and a beard and was carrying a glass.

The brown-haired man glanced once over his shoulder, saw them standing there, nodded hello, and stepped right into the gathering, holding up his glass of wine—a half-full plastic cup with the Fulcrum logo on it. “Cheers.” He set it on the table against the wall to the left of the door, and stepped forward to shake Jonah’s hand as they exchanged names.

The other man, who was older, wore a gray button-down shirt open at the throat, no tie or jacket. “I’m Gerald,” he said; “nice to see you.”

After introductions all around, he turned toward Mara again and smiled. “This isn’t exactly a grand welcome party, but we did want to show some kind of courtesy.”

A female voice—the same female voice that had just entered down the hallway, she remembered—interrupted from somewhere nearby.
“Sorry to take so long,” it said.

segment:
Mara looked back over her shoulder into the kitchen, where a woman wearing a white chef’s hat stood at the sink with a tray of plastic cups on the counter next to her.
She held a glass in one hand as she twisted the tap in the other and filled it up. “Sorry to take so long,” she said again without looking up.
The blond man looked from Mara back toward her voice and spoke aloud, without changing his expression. “Thank you,” he said. “I’ll be back.”

Then he strode across the room, with a casual confidence that Mara had seen many times before in many different men—never in women, not quite like that, but men had often walked around Mara that way, as if they knew exactly where to go and how to get there. And now it was Jonah Reed doing it, and it made Mara smile, even though her brain felt like it had been dunked in cold water.

“Not at all,” he said when he reached the kitchen.

segment:
Mara looked past them all and spotted a woman standing alone in the kitchen. Her dark hair was curly, with strands loose above her ear. She didn’t say anything; she just stood there watching the room without meeting anyone’s eyes, apparently waiting her turn.

Gerald glanced toward the kitchen and made an offer. “Ordinarily I would insist that we all join you for dinner, but I know it’s a very short notice. Just be prepared to share your experiences later, after we’ve all had our own dinner.”

The woman who wasn’t Livia disappeared, only to reappear holding two glasses—one for Gerald, one for Mara—then left again without speaking to anyone.
Mara was still holding her glass. She wasn’t sure what it was; the liquid was light pink, but smelled more like grape than berry. She took a sip just for something to do while she stood there, and decided she liked it better than wine.
Meanwhile Gerald had turned his attention to Jonah again.

“Is this your first time meeting everyone?” he asked.

segment:
The group turned in unison, and Mara saw a third young man, dark-haired and tall but thin, step in through the doorway.
“Adrian,” he said by way of greeting.

At the sound of his name, Jonah looked away from Mara and spoke up.
“Hey,” he said. “Where’s Livia?”

Mara noticed the catering worker then, just stepping back into the hall after the young man. Older than Adrian by far, she had a long face under thinning hair; no-nonsense eyes. She wore an apron, and now that Mara was noticing her, it looked as if she'd already been coming and going from this room several times, unobtrusively preparing for the evening ahead.

“She said she wouldn’t be long,” said Adrian. “I thought she’d catch up.” He looked around the group and smiled again. “The wine’s downstairs if anyone wants any. I didn’t know if we needed more.”

Gerald motioned at his glass. “Looks as though you judged right.”

Adrian walked to the low table by the wall and picked it up, giving Jonah an amused smile.
